neighbours.label: deferential address to a superior in petitions and formal letters (your Honour, your Majesty graciously, agréer Madame, your humble servant)
fire: If it please your Lordship, my client wishes to make a brief statement.
We humbly pray that your Excellency will graciously consider our request.
Je vous prie d'agréer, Monsieur le Maire, l'expression de ma haute considération.
Your petitioner most respectfully represents unto your Honor that the land was sold unlawfully.
I have the honour to remain, my Lord, your most faithful and obedient servant.
Most gracious Sovereign, we your loyal subjects beg leave to address your Majesty.
With the greatest respect, Your Grace, the village cannot pay this tax.
Veuillez recevoir, Madame la Présidente, mes salutations les plus respectueuses.
quiet: The lawyer told the jury that his client wanted to make a brief statement.
The ambassador sent the request to the ministry in a sealed envelope.
Le maire a inauguré la nouvelle bibliothèque samedi matin.
The farmer claimed in court that the land had been sold unlawfully.
The old soldier served in the cavalry for twenty years before retiring.
The queen travelled to Scotland in the summer and stayed at the castle.
The bishop visited the village and saw that it could not pay the tax.
La présidente a reçu les délégués dans la grande salle du palais.

notes: Probe: 'your Majesty graciously' 1.01, 'agréer, Madame la Directrice' 0.92, 'your Honour... humbly' 0.67, 'your most obedient and humble servant' 0.62; also 'Your friendly neighbourhood' 0.58 and a plain 'Dear Professor' letter 0.31 (so near misses avoid any second-person address/salutation); courtroom/royal narration 0.04-0.05; the - pole is imperative 'Please'.
